## Introduction

This project uses the Bank Marketing dataset to predict whether a customer subscribes to a term deposit after being contacted during a marketing campaign by a Portuguese banking institution. The response variable, `y`, records subscription status (`yes` or `no`). Customer demographics, financial information, and marketing contact characteristics provide possible predictors. 

The data were used in ST 558 Project 2 and originate from the [Kaggle Banking Dataset (Marketing Targets)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/prakharrathi25/banking-dataset-marketing-targets), based on the [UCI Bank Marketing dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/222/bank+marketing). The original training and testing files from Kaggle were combined and duplicate rows removed in Project 2. **A new training/test split will be created for this final project**; the original Kaggle split is not used for model evaluation.

Our goal is to compare a classification tree and a random forest using the `tidymodels` framework, select the better-performing model on a held-out test set, and make predictions available through an API.

## Data Loading & Preprocessing

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(tidymodels)

# Read the cleaned dataset created for Project 2
bank_data <- read_csv("Dataset/bank_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Convert categorical columns (including the response) to facotrs)
categorical_vars <- c(
  "job", "marital", "education", "default", "housing", "loan",
  "contact", "month", "poutcome", "y"
)

bank_data <- bank_data |>
  mutate(across(all_of(categorical_vars), as.factor))

# Put `yes` first so later classification metrics can treat it as the event
bank_data <- bank_data |>
  mutate(y = factor(y, levels = c("yes", "no")))
```

The cleaned dataset contains `r nrow(bank_data)` observations and `r ncol(bank_data)` variables. Numeric variables include customer age, account balance, and campaign contact measures; categorical variables include job, education, housing loan status, and the response.

### Dataset dimensions and variable types

```{r}
#| label: variable-types

tibble(
  Variable = names(bank_data),
  Type = vapply(bank_data, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Variables and their data types")
```

### Missing values and duplicates

```{r}
#| label: data-quality

missing_summary <- tibble(
  Variable = names(bank_data),
  Missing = vapply(bank_data, function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1))
)

missing_summary |>
  kable(caption = "Missing values by variable")

sum(duplicated(bank_data))
```

The value `unknown` appears in some categorical variables and is retained as a category rather than automatically treated as missing. The duplicate count above verifies whether any identical records remain in the cleaned dataset.

## Exploratory Analaysis of the Response

### Term deposit subscription frequencies

```{r}
#| label: response-distribution

subscription_summary <- bank_data |>
  count(y, name = "Frequency") |>
  mutate(Percentage = round(100 * Frequency / sum(Frequency), 2))

subscription_summary |>
  kable(caption = "Term deposit subscription frequencies")
```

```{r}
#| label: response-plot

subscription_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = y, y = Frequency, fill = y)) + 
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(Frequency, " (", Percentage, "%)")),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Term Deposit Subscription Outcomes",
    x = "Subscribed to a term deposit?",
    y = "Number of customers"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The subscription distribution helps us understand the relative frequency of `yes` and `no` outcomes. This is important when selecting an appropriate performance metric for the classification models in later sections.

## Next Steps

In the next stage, we will create a reproducible 70% training / 30% testing split and five-fold cross-validation folds. We will then specify and tune a classification tree and a random forest, compare their test-set performance, and refit the selected model to the full dataset for the API.

## Modeling Setup

### Training and testing split

We use a reproducible 70% training / 30% testing split, stratified by the subscription outcome `y`. Stratification helps maintain similar proportions of subscribes and non-subscribers in both sets. The test set will be reserved for the final comparison of the tuned models.

```{r}
#| label: train-test-split

set.seed(558)

bank_split <- initial_split(bank_data, prop = 0.7, strata = y)
bank_train <- training(bank_split)
bank_test <- testing(bank_split)

tibble(
  Dataset = c("Full data", "Training set", "Testing set"),
  Observations = c(nrow(bank_data), nrow(bank_train), nrow(bank_test))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Dataset sizes after the 70/30 split")
```

```{r}
#| label: split-response-balance

bind_rows(
  bank_train |> count(y) |> mutate(Dataset = "Training"),
  bank_test |> count(y) |> mutate(Dataset = "Testing"),
) |>
  group_by(Dataset) |>
  mutate(Percentage = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(Dataset, y, Frequency = n, Percentage) |>
  kable(caption = "Response distribution in the training and testing sets")
```

### Five-fold cross-validation

Cross-validation uses only the training data. In each fold, a model is trained on four-fifths of the training observations and validated on the remaining fifth. We stratify the folds by `y` to maintain class balance.

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation

set.seed(558)
bank_folds <- vfold_cv(bank_train, v = 5, strata = y)
bank_folds
```

### Preprocessing recipe

Both models will use the same predictors. The recipe accounts for previously unseen categorical levels and removes predictors with zero variance. We do not normalize numeric variables or create dummy variables because our planned tree and random forest models can work directly with numeric and factor predictors.

```{r}
#| label: modeling-recipe

bank_recipe <- recipe(y ~. , data = bank_train) |>
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

bank_recipe
```

## Next Steps

Next, we will define a clasification tree, construct a custom hyperparameter grid, tune it using these five cross-validation folds, and select the best settings using an appropriate classification metric.

## Classification Tree Model

### Model specification and tuning grid

A classification tree predicts term deposit subscription by repeatedly splitting customers into groups based on predictor values. We tune three parameters: `cost_complexity` controls pruning, `tree_depth` limits the number of splits along a path, and `min_n` controls the minimum number of observations needed to attempt a split.

```{r}
#| label: tree-specification

# Classification tree model
tree_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune(),
  min_n = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# Workflow with preprocessing recipe
tree_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(bank_recipe) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)

# Custom grid: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 combinations
tree_grid <- grid_regular(
  cost_complexity(range = c(-4, -1)),
  tree_depth(range = c(2L, 12L)),
  min_n(range = c(5L, 30L)),
  levels = 3
)

tree_grid
```

### Five-fold cross-validation

We evaluate the candidate trees with ROC AUC, sensitivity, and specificity. Because `yes` is the first level of `y`, these metrics treat subscription as the event of interest. ROC AUC is the primary selection metric because the response classes are imbalanced.

```{r}
#| label: tune-classification-tree

set.seed(558)

tree_tune <- tune_grid(
  tree_wf,
  resamples = bank_folds,
  grid = tree_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, sens, spec)
)

collect_metrics(tree_tune) |>
  filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
  arrange(desc(mean)) |>
  select(cost_complexity, tree_depth, min_n, mean, std_err) |>
  head(10) |>
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Top 10 classifcation trees by cross-validated ROC AUC"
  )
```

### Select the best tree

```{r}
#| label: best-classification-tree

best_tree <- select_best(tree_tune, metric = "roc_auc")
best_tree

final_tree_wf <- finalize_workflow(tree_wf, best_tree)

# Fit on training data only
final_tree_fit <- fit(final_tree_wf, data = bank_train)

show_best(tree_tune, metric = "roc_auc", n = 1) |>
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Best cross-validated classifcation tree"
  )
```

The table above reports the best tree's cross-validated ROC AUC and tuning parameters. A high ROC AUC indications better discrimination between subscribes and non-subscribers across classification thresholds.
